sources.title: World Action Models Enable Continual Imitation Learning with Recurrent Generative Replays

The extraction's image omission was addressed by inspecting the supplied PDF figures and tables. All five supplied text chunks were read individually; no supplied body or appendix section was omitted.

Only arXiv:2606.27374v1, dated 25 June 2026, was supplied and reviewed. Title and author identities match the catalog; catalog surname-first formatting is the only author-list difference. No later revision or separate edition was inspected.
Code, external project pages and separately linked references were not inspected; no experiments were reproduced.

synopsis: REGEN reuses a world-action policy to generate rehearsal trajectories for old instructions while learning a new task. Current-task observations seed recurrent prediction; synthetic observation-action pairs then supplement new demonstrations. Retention improves substantially over sequential fine-tuning, but real replay generally remains stronger, and plausible imagined outcomes can disagree with executed actions.

problem.text: A pretrained robot policy must acquire new tasks without retaining earlier demonstrations. Only earlier task instructions remain available. Ordinary fine-tuning provides no old-task supervision, while experience replay violates this information constraint. REGEN asks whether the policy's own joint action-and-observation generator can provide usable replacement supervision.

contributions.text: REGEN turns an existing WAM into its own recurrent replay generator, avoiding a separately trained dynamics model and stored old demonstrations.

The authors demonstrate improved retention in LIBERO and physical manipulation, then identify visual degradation and action-observation inconsistency as bottlenecks. Their priority claim of being the first such framework is an author claim, not independently established here.

inputs: Current-task RGB observations from primary and wrist cameras, robot proprioception and demonstrations
Previous-task language instructions and the previous-stage WAM checkpoint
outputs: Synthetic observation-action trajectories for previous tasks
An adapted policy jointly predicting action chunks, future observations and a reward/progress value

steps.name: Encode a joint prediction problem
steps.detail: Cosmos-Policy starts from Cosmos-Predict2-2B. Wan2.1 tokenizes images and pretrained T5-XXL encodes instructions. Normalized actions and proprioception become latent frames; one latent diffusion model handles actions, future observations and reward.

steps.name: Seed the old instruction with available observations
steps.detail: For each previous instruction, use real current-task observations for the first H timesteps. The instruction selects the old behavior while the visual context supplies the scene. This assumes the scene contains objects needed by the old task.

steps.name: Feed predictions back at the correct horizon
steps.detail: For t≥H, use the observation predicted at t−H. The algorithm advances t by one and stores only the first action of each predicted chunk. Figure 2 simplifies this pipeline to H=1; experiments use H=16.

steps.name: Stop and assemble replay
steps.detail: Stop at the maximum horizon or when three consecutive progress predictions exceed 0.99 and at least one reaches 1.0. Aggregate synthetic pairs across old tasks, then train on their union with current demonstrations.

training.text: The base stage uses 10K iterations; each subsequent stage uses 2K from the preceding checkpoint, with ten pseudo-trajectories per previous task. Appendix A.1 describes joint latent denoising under a flow-matching objective; Eq. (4) gives the replay update abstractly as behavioral cloning.

Table 6 specifies Adam at peak learning rate 10^-4, 1,000 warm-up steps, 30,000 cosine-decay steps, batch size 40 per GPU, four GPUs and 12 accumulation steps. Inputs are 224×224, actions seven-dimensional and proprioception nine-dimensional; augmentations are random crop, color jitter and Gaussian blur.

inference.text: Replay generation uses model predictions without simulator interaction or robot execution. Table 6 specifies five denoising steps for actions and one for observations/value. Robot evaluation executes the adapted policy; the reward head's imagined completion signal is not physical success verification. The supplied paper does not fully specify deployment action scheduling.

equations.explanation: Eq. (1): πθ is the parameterized WAM, conditioned on current observation o_t and instruction ℓ. H is the action-chunk horizon; the three predictions are actions, a future observation and a reward/progress estimate in [0,1].

equations.expression: o_t^{\mathrm{in}}=\begin{cases}o_t,&0\le t<H,\\\tilde o_t,&H\le t\le T_{\max},\end{cases}\qquad(\tilde a_{t-H:t},\tilde o_t)\sim\pi_\theta(\cdot\mid o_{t-H}^{\mathrm{in}},\ell_i)
equations.explanation: Eq. (2): o_t^in is the replay input and ℓ_i an earlier task's instruction. Real observations initialize the pipeline; subsequent inputs come from predictions H steps earlier. T_max bounds generation. The sampling relation applies to the recurrent branch.

Eq. (4): D_k contains new-task demonstrations, R_k generated old-task trajectories, and L_BC denotes the behavioral-cloning loss. The mixed dataset supplies both acquisition and rehearsal supervision; this compact expression does not enumerate implementation-level loss weights.

results.setting: Six base tasks, four sequential additions, 50 demonstrations/task; 50 randomized trials per observed task after each stage.
results.interpretation: Generated replay improves retention substantially. ER uses stored demonstrations and RAR simulator interaction, so their information/access budgets differ. RAR actually exceeds ER here despite the prose broadly calling ER strongest.

results.setting: Same six-plus-four protocol and randomized evaluation as Object.
results.comparison: Seq-FT: 90.6 / 100 / 10.3; ER: 94.0 / 7.2 / 92.4. Table 2 instead reports REGEN NBT 38.7, with FWT/AUC unchanged.
results.interpretation: Acquisition is preserved while retention improves, but the remaining ER gap is large. The conflicting NBT entries remain unresolved and must not be averaged or silently substituted.

results.task: LIBERO-Spatial continual imitation learning with prior configurations
results.setting: Same task count and evaluation protocol, but REGEN† seeds generation using previous-task object configurations.
results.interpretation: Strong retention under a modified initialization assumption; this is not a demonstration that current-task observations alone suffice for every suite.

results.setting: Carrot-in-bowl → carrot-on-plate → eggplant-in-bowl; 50 demonstrations/task at 15 Hz; ten randomized trials/task and two adaptation stages.
results.metric: FWT ↑ / NBT ↓ / AUC ↑ from the reported partial-scoring protocol
results.interpretation: Physical experiments support improved scored performance. Appendix B.3 awards 50 points for touching the object and 50 for reaching the goal; these aggregates must not be presented as binary task-completion percentages.

results.setting: Replay count on LIBERO-Object; stopping criterion on LIBERO-Goal.
results.metric: FWT / NBT / AUC for replay count; PSNR ↑ for stopping
results.value: Five → ten replays: 96.5/33/62.5 → 96.1/31/62.3. Goal-reward stopping PSNR: 20.3.
results.interpretation: More replay modestly reduces NBT without improving AUC. The ten-replay row differs from Table 1 without explanation. Higher PSNR under early stopping does not establish improved executed success.

results.setting: LIBERO-Goal pseudo-trajectories across four continual stages; predicted actions executed in the simulator.
results.value: Imagined / grounded: S1 83/42, S2 65/20, S3 62/30, S4 44/38.
results.comparison: Each stage compares visual predictions with execution of predicted actions.
results.interpretation: The generation can depict success that its actions do not realize. Figure 5 diagnoses inconsistency, not a guarantee that improving image fidelity alone would close the retention gap.

limitations.text: Recursive visual artifacts accumulate within rollouts and over adaptation stages. The authors associate declining PSNR with forgetting and hypothesize weakened action-observation alignment; the diagnostic comparison does not isolate a single causal mechanism.

FWT here is average acquisition performance, not improvement over an untrained baseline. Main result tables lack uncertainty across training seeds. Figure 4's lower representation drift for REGEN is supportive but cannot independently establish task success.

reproduction.text: Reproduction requires the specified Cosmos/Wan/T5 components, camera/proprioception preprocessing, fixed task orders, generated replay and stagewise checkpoints. Preserve the appendix's partial scoring and Spatial exception. Table 6 gives GPU count but no GPU model, runtime or software versions.

Unspecified details include mixed-data sampling weights, which pretrained modules are frozen, exact PSNR reference/alignment, and how the learning-rate schedule restarts across stages. Also resolve NBT table conflicts, base-stage aggregation in the metric formulas, and zero acquisition-score handling before comparing implementations.

reasoning.text: The recorded One Model × Joint prediction classification is supported by the shared latent diffusion architecture for action, observation and reward generation, not merely by joint training. REGEN adds continual rehearsal around that WAM; it does not introduce a separate inverse-dynamics action extractor or an inference-time planning search. Generated observations actively condition replay generation.

discussionQuestions: Would state-action-consistent replay improve retention more than a PSNR-matched visual improvement? (ev-diagnostics, ev-action-mismatch)
How far can instruction-only retention extend when required old-task objects are absent from current scenes? (ev-spatial)

evidence.location: PDF p. 1, title block and arXiv margin stamp
evidence.detail: The title and five authors match the catalog. The PDF identifies arXiv:2606.27374v1 [cs.RO], 25 June 2026, and the Department of Computer Science, University of North Carolina at Charlotte, United States.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 1–2, Abstract, Section 1 and Figure 1; pp. 3–4, Section 4.1
evidence.detail: REGEN addresses continual imitation learning when previous-task instructions remain available but previous action-observation demonstrations do not. Generated replay is mixed with current-task demonstrations.

evidence.location: PDF p. 3, Section 3, Eq. (1); p. 14, Appendix A.1
evidence.detail: Cosmos-Policy uses a latent video diffusion model initialized from Cosmos-Predict2-2B. Wan2.1 encodes images and pretrained T5-XXL encodes language; actions and proprioception are normalized to [-1,+1] and converted into latent frames. The model jointly denoises action, future-observation and reward latents under the described flow-matching objective.

evidence.location: PDF p. 4, Section 4.2, Figure 2 and Eq. (2); p. 15, Algorithm 1, lines 4–15
evidence.detail: For t<H the input is a current-task real observation; afterward it is the observation predicted H timesteps earlier. Algorithm 1 increments t by one. Figure 2 illustrates H=1; its caption calls the left side unrolled although the explicit unrolled sequence is on the right.

evidence.location: PDF p. 5, Section 4.2, Termination, Eqs. (3)–(4); p. 15, Algorithm 1, lines 12–25
evidence.detail: Generation stops at the maximum horizon or after three consecutive reward predictions above 0.99 with at least one reaching 1.0. Each replay entry pairs the input observation with the first predicted action. The policy is then updated using current real data plus generated replay.

The base model trains for 10K iterations and each continual stage for 2K, generating 10 replays per previous task. Table 6 specifies 224×224 images, action dimension 7, proprioception dimension 9, H=16, Adam, learning rate 10^-4, 1,000 warm-up steps, 30,000 cosine-decay steps, four GPUs, batch size 40 per GPU, accumulation 12, crop/color-jitter/Gaussian-blur augmentation, and five action versus one observation/value denoising steps.

evidence.location: PDF p. 5, Section 5.1, FWT, NBT and AUC definitions
evidence.detail: FWT averages diagonal task-acquisition scores r_n,n; NBT averages later relative drops (r_n,n-r_p,n)/r_n,n; AUC averages each task's scores from its acquisition onward. Higher FWT/AUC and lower NBT are preferred.

evidence.location: PDF p. 6, Section 5.2, Setting and Baseline Methods; pp. 15–16, Appendix B.1–B.3
evidence.detail: Each LIBERO suite has ten tasks and 50 demonstrations per task; six tasks form the base stage and four arrive sequentially. The appendix gives fixed task orders shared across methods. Evaluation uses 50 randomized trials per observed task after each stage. ER retains real demonstrations; RAR collects simulator rollouts.

evidence.location: PDF p. 6, Table 1, REGEN, Seq-FT, ER and RAR rows across all three suites
PDF p. 7, Section 5.2 continuation, paragraph explaining REGEN†
evidence.detail: Spatial replay is initialized with object configurations sampled from previous tasks because required objects must be present. The authors state that trajectories involving absent objects cannot be reliably synthesized.

evidence.location: PDF p. 7, Table 2 and VLA vs. WAM Continual Learning
evidence.detail: Table 2 reports π0.5 Seq-FT at 96.8/88/35.5 and Cosmos-Policy REGEN at 90.6/38.7/40.8 on Goal. REGEN's NBT 38.7 differs from 44.9 in Table 1, with unchanged FWT/AUC; no reconciliation is supplied.

evidence.location: PDF p. 7, Section 5.3, Table 3 and Figure 3; p. 16, Appendix B.3, Real-world
evidence.detail: The xArm7 learns carrot-in-bowl, carrot-on-plate, then eggplant-in-bowl with 50 demonstrations per task at 15 Hz and ten randomized evaluation trials per task. Table 3 gives Seq-FT FWT/NBT/AUC 50/96.3/13.8 and REGEN 80/60.5/53.8. Appendix B.3 awards 50 points for touching the target and 50 for reaching the goal.

evidence.location: PDF p. 8, Figure 4 and Section 5.4, Action representation drift and Visualization of predicted actions
evidence.detail: After the first continual stage, mean action-latent centroid L2 distances across six base tasks are 0.30 for Seq-FT, 0.04 for ER and 0.12 for REGEN. The accompanying XY trajectory example shows REGEN closer to the demonstration than Seq-FT.

evidence.location: PDF p. 8, Section 5.4, Number of replays; p. 9, Table 4
evidence.detail: For Object, five replays yield FWT/NBT/AUC 96.5/33/62.5 and ten yield 96.1/31/62.3. The ten-replay row differs from the main Object result; the supplied text does not explain the setting or run difference.

evidence.location: PDF p. 8, Section 5.4, Termination criterion; p. 9, Table 5
evidence.detail: Goal-reward stopping yields reported PSNR 20.3 versus 18.4 for fixed horizon 200 and 19.5 for fixed horizon 150 on LIBERO-Goal. Table 5 labels these horizons H, although the method uses H for chunk length and T_max for maximum rollout length.

evidence.location: PDF p. 9, Figure 5, all panels, and Section 6
evidence.detail: Generated-frame PSNR declines across stages; REGEN NBT remains above RAR. Imagined versus simulator-grounded success percentages are 83/42, 65/20, 62/30 and 44/38 for stages 1–4. The authors hypothesize that degraded observations weaken state-action alignment.

evidence.location: PDF p. 18, Figure 6 and caption; p. 19, Figure 7 and caption
evidence.detail: Figure 6 pairs green expert frames with blue generated frames for four tasks. Figure 7 compares current-task, Seq-FT and REGEN rollouts on selected previous tasks in Goal, Object, Spatial and real-world settings.

evidence.location: PDF p. 20, Figure 8 and caption; p. 17, Appendix C.3
evidence.detail: Generated sequences for putting the bowl on top of the cabinet become progressively blurrier across the four continual stages.

evidence.location: PDF p. 21, Figure 9 and caption; p. 17, Appendix C.4
evidence.detail: For pushing a plate and placing a black bowl, the upper green-bordered imagined sequences appear successful while the lower red-bordered simulator executions fail to realize the imagined states.
